questions.question: How does full translation differ from total translation?
questions.solution_html:
• Related but distinct concepts in Catford's theory. Full translation - extent of the translation
  • process - every part of the Source Language (SL) text is subjected to translation -replaced by Target
  • Language (TL) material - focuses on the breadth of the text being translated. Total translation is a
  • technical term - involves the comprehensive replacement of SL text - specifically entails replacing SL
  • grammar and lexis with equivalent TL grammar and lexis - includes the consequential replacement of
  • SL phonology/graphology with non-equivalent TL phonology/graphology - delves into the specific
  • levels of language being addressed - highlighting that not all linguistic levels achieve equivalence
  • especially phonological and graphological aspects.
questions.final_answer: especially phonological and graphological aspects

questions.question: Why does Catford make a distinction between the terms, 'text' and 'textual material'? Explain.
questions.solution_html:
• material'? Explain.
  • Distinguishes between ‘textual material’ and ‘text’ to highlight that not every part of the Source
  • Language (SL) text is translated into the Target Language (TL). ‘textual material’ emphasizes the
  • specific segments that undergo translation, acknowledging that some elements may remain untranslated
  • or be replaced with non-equivalent material - distinction allows for a more nuanced understanding of the
  • translation process, where only certain parts of the text are actively replaced, while others are simply
  • transferred or retained in their original form - Catford points out that translation is not a wholesale
  • substitution of one language for another but involves selective replacement based on equivalence and
  • contextual considerations - underscores the complexity of translation - maintaining the integrity and
  • meaning of the original text may require leaving some elements untranslated to preserve local color or
  • due to the absence of direct equivalents in the TL.
